title: The long story of a past Buddha (Kern ch. 7)
word: The long story of a past Buddha
hookLine: a Buddha of ages past and his sixteen sons who taught

cards: Chapter seven of the Lotus looks back, so far back that the sutra needs a whole picture just to say how long ago. The Diamond Sutra ground a world to dust to ask what a heap is.
The Lotus grinds a world to dust to measure time. Carry the dust across the worlds, and let fall one speck only after crossing a great stretch of them, until the dust is gone.
The time since this story is longer than that.

teach.b: Kern gives the old Buddha's name as Mahabhijnajnanabhibhu. He sat at the seat of awakening, and for a long time full awakening did not come. He stayed seated, steady, until at last it did.

Before he left home, the story says, he had been a prince with sixteen sons. When they heard their father had awakened, they left their toys and palaces to honor him, their family following behind, and asked him to teach.
Kings of the heavens came too, from every direction, offering their palaces and asking the same. Their father taught the early teachings first, and many were freed.
Later the sixteen sons, now young monks, asked him for more, and he taught them this very sutra, the Lotus.
Then he went into a long meditation, and while he sat, each son took a seat and taught the Lotus to the crowds, in detail, for a long time. Here is the turn.
Those sixteen sons, the Buddha says, are all Buddhas now, teaching in different directions. One of them, in the west, is called Amitayus.
And the sixteenth son is me. I am the one who taught you then. The listeners in front of him today are the same beings he taught as that young monk, ages ago.
The long story isn't a detour. It tells the disciples why they are here.

The teaching has a lineage older than they can picture, passed from father to sons, from sons to listeners, and they were already in it. Yesterday's promises weren't new. They were old seeds coming up.

how: Some Lotus Sutra readers in East Asia study chapter seven's story of the ancient Buddha and his sixteen sons as the account of the Buddha's long bond with his hearers; some readers link the mention of Amitayus in the west to Pure Land devotion.

games.q: what does “the long story of a past buddha” mean?
o: the story of the Buddha's own childhood as a prince
the Buddha's tale of a past Buddha and his sixteen sons
a list of every Buddha who taught before this one

p: taught the Lotus while he sat

s: the past Buddha awakened the moment he sat down
the sutra says that for a long time full awakening did not come; he stayed seated until it did.
the sixteen sons taught the Lotus while their father was in meditation
each took a seat and taught it to the crowds.
the Buddha says the people listening to him now are new to his teaching
he says they are the same beings he taught as the sixteenth son, ages ago.

games.q: you are one of the sixteen princes. you hear that your father, who left home, has awakened. what do you do?
o: stay in the palace and send a gift
leave your toys and go to him, and ask him to teach
wait for him to come home
games.why: the sons go to honor him and ask him to teach; later, as young monks, they teach the Lotus themselves.

practice: Think of something you know how to do, a craft, a song, a recipe, a way of praying or sitting, and ask who taught it to you, then who taught them. Follow the chain back, face by face, until the faces blur.
Rest at the edge of what you can see, grateful to everyone in the line, known and unknown.

wordCard.voice: The long story of a past Buddha. In chapter seven, a Buddha of ages past teaches the Lotus to his sixteen sons; the sixteenth is the Buddha telling the story. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: former connection, ancient bond; the name of chapter seven in Kern's Sanskrit text.

carryVoice: Your line: sixteen sons. The teacher in the story was the teacher telling it. Until tomorrow.
